演奏時將葫蘆絲垂直持握，左手拇指與前三指按主管上方四孔，右手前三指按其餘孔；嘴唇: You hold the hulusi vertically. The left thumb and the first three fingers cover the top four holes of the main pipe, and the first three fingers of the right hand cover the rest; the lips close around the blowhole and send in a fairly strong airstream. The main pipe plays the melody and the side pipes can sound a drone, stopped with a cloth plug or a finger when needed. Beginners first learn where the fingerholes are and how to keep the airstream steady, then practise slurs, slides, vibrato and bending the pitch. Each instrument is fixed in one key and has a narrow range, which suits it to playing solo.
葫蘆絲主要見於中國雲南、緬甸撣邦與印度阿薩姆等地的傣族、阿昌族、德昂族、佤族、布: The hulusi is heard mainly in the music of the Dai, Achang, De'ang, Wa and Blang peoples of Yunnan in China, Shan State in Myanmar and Assam in India. Traditionally it can accompany dance, and because it is quiet it is more often played solo. In its usual scoring the main pipe plays the melody while the side pipes sound a single note or a drone to make harmony. Today it has spread across China into popular music and school teaching, and European composers and players have taken it up. You can listen to 《月光下的鳳尾竹》 (Moonlight over the Phoenix-tail Bamboo) by Shi Guangnan, usually treated as its signature piece, and to teaching pieces such as 《龍的傳人》 (Descendants of the Dragon) and 《荷塘月色》 (Moonlight over the Lotus Pond).
葫蘆絲原主要用於緬甸撣邦、中國雲南西南部與印度東北阿薩姆的少數民族，傣族、阿昌族: The hulusi was originally used mainly by the minority peoples of Shan State in Myanmar, south-west Yunnan in China and Assam in north-east India; the Dai, Achang, De'ang, Wa and Blang all play it. It later became widespread throughout China and also passed among the indigenous peoples of Assam, and in Vietnam it is called 葫蘆簫, the gourd flute. In recent years European composers and players have adopted it, and factories and workshops in Chinese cities produce it in quantity. Concert models add a brass windchest, keyed side pipes and a second main pipe, extending the range and the harmony; other versions have keyed fingerholes that widen the range by several octaves. 《月光下的鳳尾竹》 (Moonlight over the Phoenix-tail Bamboo), written in 1979, has become its signature piece.
葫蘆絲為自由簧氣鳴樂器，主管音色純淨、柔和並帶簧片感，近似巴烏與單簧管。傳統音域: The hulusi is a free-reed aerophone. The main pipe has a clean, soft tone with a reedy edge, close to the bawu and the clarinet. Its traditional range is about an octave, or nine notes, usually in a pentatonic or hexatonic scale, and the side pipes can sound a drone; keyed versions extend the range by several octaves. When it sounds, the reed and the air column couple, and pitch is decided mainly by the length of the pipe — unlike the accordion or the harmonica, where the reed's own frequency dominates. It needs a fairly strong airstream, yet its overall volume is low, so it is mostly played solo; the side pipes can be stopped with cloth plugs or by covering holes, to control how thick the harmony is.
葫蘆絲的風箱多用小雙肚葫蘆或瓶頸葫蘆製成，三根管通常為竹管，部分記載稱金竹管。吹: The windchest of the hulusi is usually a small double-bellied gourd or a bottle-necked gourd, and the three pipes are normally bamboo, some accounts saying golden bamboo. The mouthpiece can be a hole opened at the end of the gourd's neck, or a small bamboo pipe or short wooden pipe inserted there. The sound source is a thin reed set into the wall of the pipe near its closed end; reeds are of copper, bamboo, bronze or silver, and modern examples also set a copper reed in a plastic frame. Bamboo pipes and gourd were traditionally fixed with hardened beeswax; today an adhesive is usual, sometimes with rosin, vegetable oil, insect resin and ash added. The lower ends of the side pipes can be muted with cloth plugs and thread. The materials of the remaining parts are not recorded.
葫蘆絲（Hulusi）為自由簧氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號: The hulusi is a free-reed aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 412.3. The hulusi is a free-reed aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 412.3. A gourd serves as the windchest and three bamboo pipes are inserted into it; the central main pipe is drilled with fingerholes and plays the melody, while the side pipes generally sound a drone and may be reduced to one or kept only as ornament. The player holds it vertically and blows a fairly strong airstream into the mouthpiece at the top, so the main pipe and the side pipes sound together and make harmony. Traditionally it is widespread in Yunnan in China, Shan State in Myanmar and Assam in India, where the Dai, Achang, De'ang, Wa and Blang peoples use it and it accompanies dance; it later became popular all over China and was taken up by European composers and players.
